t: Your syllabus needs an enemy

t: The Problem with Transferable Skills
q: Despite the current vogue for attempting to teach transferable skills rather than specific knowledge, the best evidence we have indicates that it is not possible.

t: The Skill That Got Me Promoted Was the One I Had to Give Up
q: Someone once told me, plainly, that the thing I was best at was the thing that would keep me from being promoted.

Sit with how that lands when you are twenty-eight and everything you are proud of is your own flawlessness. I was not being told to improve. I was being told to give up the one thing that had gotten me everything so far. It felt less like advice and more like being told the ground I was standing on was the problem.

That thought is the whole reason this is hard. In the moment you finally loosen your grip and something goes wrong, it does not feel like a lesson about growth. It feels like proof that you should never have loosened it in the first place.

If I could not let go, I could not scale. And if I could not scale, I could not lead. I would spend my whole career as the most reliable individual performer in the building, valuable and capped, doing more and more of the same work, never trusted with more, because everything I touched required me to touch it. Perfection is an individual sport.

When you check everything yourself, every error feels equally fatal. A typo and a broken model feel the same in your stomach, because your name is on all of it and you cannot tell the difference between what matters and what does not. You have no sense of proportion, because proportion is a thing you can only develop from a little distance.
It felt like losing myself. It was the beginning of actually being able to lead.

t: The Most Expensive Assumption We Ever Made
q: We called them digital natives. Their the digital generation, they just get technology or my kid knows how to use my phone better than I do. This is what many of us assumed 15 years ago when smart phones and social media started to encroach upon our daily lives. If kids were born knowing how to navigate technology, then we didn't have to teach it. We could hand them the device and step back.

What kids actually have is comfort — fast thumbs, no fear of the interface. What they don't have, unless someone teaches it, is comprehension of what the technology is doing to them and for them. Comfort and comprehension look identical from across the room. They are not the same thing, and the gap between them is exactly where a generation got hurt.

When the OECD tested fifteen-year-olds across dozens of countries on whether they could distinguish fact from opinion in what they read online, fewer than one in ten could do it reliably. These are the same students who can run three apps at once, who live on their phones, who look — from across the room — completely fluent. They could open everything. They could evaluate almost nothing.

This is the social media pattern replaying in real time. Mass adoption by kids. Minimal awareness by adults. Zero instruction in between. We have seen this exact movie, and we know the ending, and we are watching it again with the sequel.

Ask that same confident-looking student whether the answer is right, or where it came from, or what the tool quietly got wrong, or whether they should have used it at all — and you find the same gap we found with social media. They don't know that these systems generate plausible text rather than verified truth. They don't know the machine will invent a source with a straight face. Access is not understanding. It never was.
The second pillar is a refusal: don't assume fluency. Teach it. Deliberately, as curriculum, the way we would teach anything else that matters.

t: Leadership Beyond Technique
q: Leadership, no less than literary education, must be animated first by a care for advancing what is most human. To organize, to operate, to levy strategic clarity is to participate in acts of love; it is to take seriously the communal implications of thoughtful order.

When reduced to technique, performance, or the mastery of professional tools, leadership loses its magnanimous purpose. It is easily forgotten in our age of systems, strategies, dashboards, and management literature that leadership is not finally justified by productivity.

A leader who cuts corners teaches that appearances matter more than integrity. A leader who avoids hard conversations teaches that false harmony is preferable to truth. A leader who praises talent but ignores character teaches that giftedness excuses disorder. A leader who is perpetually hurried teaches that people are interruptions.

Leadership reaches its proper fulfillment only when these instruments serve a deeper inheritance: when they help create a place where truth can be spoken plainly, where good work is honored, where joy is not feigned, where dignity is preserved, where standards are clear, where burdens are shared, and where others are strengthened rather than merely used.

Leadership is therefore not only directional. It is formative. In that sense, leadership bears a deep resemblance to education. The leader is always teaching, even when no formal lesson is being given.
Leadership is proven not by how much depends upon the leader, but by how much good continues to live and grow in the people and culture under his care.

t: I Built a Team That Could Run Without Me. Then I Found Out Why.
q: We also learned early when we could afford to hire, and we hired well. The people we brought on took real ownership of their roles, in all kinds of ways I didn't expect and couldn't have done better myself.
For a long time I told that story as proof we'd built something great. And we had. But I left out the part that actually explains it. The business was easy.

That's the trap, and it's a sneaky one. When things are easy, a team that just executes looks identical to a team that could handle anything. You genuinely cannot tell them apart on a good day. You only find out which one you built when it gets hard, and by then it's a rough time to be finding out.

Good is exactly when to hand people real problems. Not just tasks to run, but things to figure out, decisions to own, messes to sort through while the stakes are still low and you can afford for it to be a little clumsy.

The point of a team that runs without you was never that they can hold things steady when it's smooth. Anyone can do that. It's that when it gets hard, they solve it, and it doesn't all come running back to you.

t: How Did the Laboratory Become the Arbiter of Learning in Classrooms?
q: It can be said that much of developmental psychology is the science of the strange behavior of children in strange situations with strange adults for the briefest periods of time" (Urie Bronfenbrenner, 1977).

Placing an individual child in strange situations, doing strange things in strange places with strange adults dressed in white coats carrying clipboards—you will have to decide for yourself whether this is the path to truth and enlightenment.

In 1979 he published his book The Ecological Model of Human Development which ushered in a new criterion for research: ecological validity. On this view, it is a mistake to believe one has found the truth about human development based on a decontextualized measurement of a behavior produced in a laboratory deliberately stripped of all other legible factors which might have influenced an outcome.

The independent variable is phonemic awareness training. The dependent variable is decoding score. The finding is a meta-analytic effect size aggregated across dozens of these studies, interpreted as a main effect: explicit phonemic awareness instruction produces better readers than business as usual. The epistemic warrant, the arbiter, is the aggregated significance test.

So what? How does one bridge the gap between the finding and the subject world we share and are interested in improving? Was Christmas a dark time of year for Little Albert from thence forward? Did the children in the Bobo doll study become more aggressive?

Determining whether direct instruction in phonemic awareness can improve decoding skills, however, is different. We do see children's great enjoyment in language play, in rhyming words, in making up sounds and words. Is it possible that direct instruction using refined protocols for manipulating phonemes could have a positive impact on decoding?

t: Claude Is Free for Teachers. Here Are Fifteen Things I Use It For.

That's a reasonable conclusion to draw from that evidence.

I don't write careful prompts. I've read the guides on how to do it and I don't do it. What I type instead is the same half-legible note I'd scribble on the back of a folder — the drills we ran, who debated whom, the four things I want on the slides — and then I upload whatever materials I already have sitting on my computer and let it work out what I meant.

The standards connection is the part that goes beyond a discount. Through Learning Commons, Claude has each state's standards along with the smaller competencies underneath them and the order students usually learn them in, so what you get back is scaffolded rather than just on topic.

t: Beyond CUBES: Rethinking How I Teach Word Problems
q: CUBES was giving my students a procedure for what to do to the words in the problem. It wasn't necessarily giving them knowledge about the mathematical structure underneath those words.

My students could circle the numbers. They could underline the question. They could box a word. And very often, they could still have absolutely no idea whether the numbers in the problem should be added, subtracted, multiplied or divided.
On high-stakes tests, keyword strategies work <50% of the time. (Powell, Namkung, & Lin, 2022)

More signaled the student to add, but they really need to subtract. The mathematical structure of that problem never changed. Both would be considered Compare problems, in schema instruction. What changed was the location of the unknown within the problem, but the student wasn't able to recognize that, because they were focused on the key word, more, that they had learned meant to add.
Instead of teaching students to ask: What operation am I supposed to do? or: What keyword tells me what to do? we can teach them to ask: What kind of mathematical relationship is happening here?

We tend to present word problems to children as though every new story is a new problem to figure out. When really it isn't. Underneath all of the names, objects, settings, and numbers are a relatively small number of mathematical structures. Those structures are called schemas. And we can explicitly teach students to recognize them.

t: Stop Arguing Your Case. Start Holding the Question.
q: I'm going to suggest a fourth way instead. I call it holding.
Trying to argue your way to change isn't likely to work. People often don't behave like rational actors.

Ghosting is what happens when leaders realize, often after one or two failed attempts, that the communication challenge is harder than anticipated. Rather than try a third time, the leader finds some way of working around the roadblock or simply accepts the status quo.
Holding is the recognition that some problems and possibilities need to be carried in the organizational atmosphere for a while before anyone can work on them.

What Rachel actually did—without necessarily knowing it—is hold the question of whether a webinar series would be valuable for the organization. She held it in her own mind, she raised it in conversation, she brought data to it when that was appropriate, and she let it develop.

t: Some Power Games That Happen in Schools
q: From my own experience, I know that power can turn people in education into self-centred individuals.

They are no longer judged by their teaching, but by their control of the teachers who work for them and their control of the school. They are rewarded for their decisiveness even if the decision they made wasn't based on consulting teachers who were affected by it.

Power tends to change the social environment around senior leaders. People laugh at their jokes more. They stop being challenged, and often their ideas are accepted too quickly. Over time, this can create a bubble where they believe their perspective is the objective truth.
Those leaders who aren't sure about leading can often slip into power games because they are scared of what could happen if they don't step in and manage and control how staff work.

Teachers can cope with high expectations, they cope with them every day. What wears them down is the sense that the rules are not stable, and that their professional worth is being assessed through a lens they cannot control.
x: The leadership bubble—where people defer, ideas go unchallenged, and the leader's perspective becomes self-confirming truth—is a normal consequence of positional power, not personal malice.

Debbie Thompson draws on 24 years in English secondary schools to analyze how senior leaders who were once excellent teachers can slip into power-game dynamics that undermine and exhaust the teachers in their charge.

Insecure leaders are most prone to power games: the gotcha observation, shifting expectations, and unpredictable standards are symptoms of leaders who manage through fear because they fear losing control.
Unpredictability is the specific mechanism that wears teachers down—high expectations can be met, but standards that shift without warning make professional competence impossible to demonstrate.

q: The Standards are poor. They are not based on evidence from cognitive science or high-quality education research. For example, they do not mention explicit teaching, cognitive load theory, the worked example effect, retrieval practice, spaced practice, or methods of checking for understanding.

This shows the Standards are based more on ideology and romantic ideas of how the author/s would like the world to be than being based on how the world actually is.

The real significance of the Arday case is that it serves as a further demonstration that the field of educational academia has lost a sense of its primary, substantive purpose: to generate and share knowledge that will improve education.

This managerialism has perverse consequences. t: From Confusion to Clarity: Creating Common Expectations for AI Use
a: Jennifer W. Shewmaker and Julie Crum
q: The challenge isn't that teachers approach AI differently but that students are left trying to decode a brand-new set of rules every time they change classes.

Students aren't always asking, 'How do I do this assignment?' More often they're wondering, 'Am I allowed to use AI for this? If so, how can I use it?' That's mental energy we want them investing in learning, not in guessing about expectations.

The real leadership challenge of the AI era—providing enough structure for both teachers and students so there is clarity rather than fear while allowing room for the flexibility needed for different fields, levels of learning, and learning outcomes.
Policies alone, however, don't always translate into clear expectations on an ordinary weekday morning. Too often, students discover the boundaries only after they've crossed them.

A principle we've been emphasizing at Lipscomb is that clarity supports learning. The important thing is that students understand the expectations before they begin an assignment, not after they've unintentionally crossed a line.

t: Your AI Policy Is a Rule, and Students Route Around Rules
q: A list of prohibitions teaches a student how to hide, not how to work.

A student who asks the bot to write the argument skips the exact struggle where learning lives. A student who writes the argument first and then asks the bot to attack it has to defend it or rethink it. It's the same tool, but one of those students got smarter.
So stop writing rules about AI and start writing the workflow. Do the thinking first, then let the machine pressure it.

A student who writes 'I used AI on this' has told you nothing. A student who writes 'I asked ChatGPT to outline counterarguments, then wrote and rejected two of them myself' has told you where she leaned and where she worked.
If honesty about AI use costs points, you have taught your class that hiding it is the correct strategy. They are very good at strategy.
Set it per assignment, not per course. 'AI allowed' across fifteen weeks means nothing when week three is a reflection and week eleven is a data analysis.
x: A prohibition-based AI policy teaches students where the lines are so they can navigate around them, not how to use AI in ways that actually build thinking.

His alternative has two parts: first, design the workflow—specify at which step in an assignment AI may enter, ensuring students do the core cognitive work before using AI to challenge or pressure their thinking.

Part two of the framework is a minimal, per-assignment disclosure standard: tool name, what was asked, and what the student did with the output—a sentence that tells an instructor far more than 'AI used here.'

t: Why Every Christian Should Read Old Books

t: Who's Really Teaching Helplessness?
q: There's a common criticism that explicit instruction creates learned helplessness by providing too much support. But if learned helplessness is the belief that your efforts won't lead to success, we should ask a different question. Who's really teaching helplessness?
Learned helplessness is not produced by too much support. It is produced by repeated failure with no path to success.

Sometimes we throw students into the deep end in the name of independence and watch them flounder. Other times, convinced they'll never be able to access the core curriculum, we lower the bar altogether and replace meaningful learning with tasks designed simply to keep them occupied. Both approaches teach the same lesson: this isn't for you.
True independence is not the absence of instruction. It is what happens after good instruction.
The goal of scaffolding is always eventual removal—but the removal has to be earned by demonstrated mastery, not imposed prematurely by ideology.
x: The common claim that explicit instruction creates learned helplessness inverts the psychology: learned helplessness results from repeated failure with no effective path forward, not from receiving support.

t: What Makes a Teacher: Everything I Wish I Learned in College
q: Nobody ever said the word dyslexia. Not once. Not in a single one of those genuinely science-based, best-practice reading courses.

Schools of education should teach dyslexia. Period. It is a reading disability that affects as many as one in five students, which means there is no version of a teaching career where you don't encounter it.

Leaving future teachers uneducated about what dyslexia is and how to address it as a tier one practitioner is the equivalent of the medical field declining to train OBGYNs in perimenopause and menopause care.

I was placed in a 6th grade classroom with 38 students. My cooperating teacher was burnt out beyond belief, and her friend stated bluntly that I had been assigned to help her. I wasn't there to learn. I was there to be a second adult in the room.

On any given day, only two percent of American adults read to a child.

The way you organize the physical space within your school speaks volumes. Ask yourself, what would each space in my school community look like if it were impossible to miss that this is a school that is invested in reading and literacy?

t: The Downside of Using Exclusion to Create Group Cohesion
q: Somewhat ironically, excluding people often creates a deeper connection and more pride in being a member. Exclusion is one of the oldest tricks in the leadership playbook, and it's worth understanding exactly how and why it works.
Nothing bonds a group faster than rejecting others or celebrating a shared sense of being chosen. That's why exclusion is so tempting for leaders in a hurry to increase group cohesion.

Over time, people start to fear being rejected by the group and excluded like the outsiders they've been taught to look down on. So, they fall in line. They become less willing to speak up about issues they disagree with, because disagreement begins to feel like disloyalty.
The very cohesion that felt so strong at the start slowly turns brittle. It holds together through fear of exclusion rather than genuine commitment.
Good leaders create belonging without making it dependent on exclusion. They resist the shortcut of an 'us' versus 'them' story, even though it is fast and effective.
The circle that holds people by fear will always be weaker than the one that holds them by choice.

Over time, exclusion-based cohesion becomes fear-based compliance: members suppress disagreement and avoid risk because crossing a line feels like risking expulsion.

The alternative is cohesion built on shared purpose and values rather than on rejection of outsiders—slower to build but producing a culture where people speak up, take risks, and remain loyal by genuine choice rather…

t: Rites of Passage
q: I traded my guitar for a gun and spent months crawling in the dirt in Southern California alongside hundreds of other young men who were intent on becoming United States Marines.
The pain in bootcamp is mundane. If you're in decent shape, it's not a problem. What is much more thorough and impactful, however, is the sustained humiliation.
Humiliation is like a good marinade before searing the meat. It makes it pliable for the work to come.

You have no first name and if you find yourself having to communicate with a drill instructor, you must only use the third person to refer to yourself. There is no 'self' now...just another Marine recruit among many.

Any infraction is rewarded with physical pain and degradation, and sometimes an added psychological element if you do something stupid: you might have to write letters to your fellow recruits' mothers, wives, and children to explain why your selfishness, incompetence, weakness, or stupidity has caused their son, husband, or father to die unnecessarily.

To succeed in this environment requires negotiating a sustainable truce between your fear of pain and humiliation, your resentment at being forced into those feelings, your own disgust with yourself for feeling them in the first place, and a prudent management of your physical capacity for suffering.

t: Jim Callaghan's Secret Garden, Fifty Years On
q: It is known as the 'Secret Garden' speech because Callaghan compared the world of education to a secret garden that elected politicians, parents and ordinary taxpayers were not allowed to have an opinion on, even when things were obviously going wrong.

Even that circumlocutory phrasing was inflammatory, and was enough to bring out the 'continental tyranny' counter argument: the general secretary of the head teachers' union compared the proposal to Nazi interference in the 1930s German curriculum.

Callaghan's speech was just a speech, and wasn't followed up by any legislation on curriculum. It was enormously influential and was frequently cited 12 years later when the Conservative government passed the landmark 1988 Education Reform Act.
It was always going to be unsustainable for education to receive so much funding from central government, but for central government to have so little say over it.

The lesson from the past is that if you devolve power and responsibility without commensurate tax-raising powers, you get problems. You risk getting irresponsible local authorities, and a meddlesome central government.

t: Every Decision Is a Prediction
q: Every map does two jobs. The first is explaining what you've already seen. The second is predicting what you haven't seen yet. People judge maps by the first. Reality judges them by the second.

You hire someone. Sitting across from them, you are making a claim: this person handles the work, and six months from now I'll be glad I picked them. That's a prediction with a date attached, and you almost certainly never say it out loud.
Reality answers, constantly, and faster than most people notice.
Without a prediction, an outcome is just something that happened. With a prediction, the same outcome becomes feedback.

That's how you and Dana can sit through identical months and walk out holding opposite conclusions, both of you honest. Neither of you was scoring anything, and impressions bend toward whatever you believed in January.

Reality 'answers' decisions constantly through events like missed handoffs, client complaints, and behavioral changes—but those answers require an explicit question (prediction) to be meaningful.
Without a written prediction, an outcome is just noise that gets absorbed into the observer's prior belief; with a prediction, the same outcome becomes signal.

t: "Fixed it."

When a problem arises, people naturally reach for the most visible cause so they can quickly move from uncertainty to action. Then they can declare it handled without uncovering any deeper, decidedly more inconvenient realities.
All the time and money in the world won't help you if you're solving the wrong problem or targeting the wrong cause.

t: Three Tenses of Sense Giving
q: The role of leadership for collective sense making is sense giving; guiding the team to interpret events and situations in a way that makes action towards educational goals more likely or more cohesive. This is not telling people what to think or presenting a narrow account of events.

Sense making is inherently retrospective; something happens and we seek to understand it: a set of academic results, patterns of pastoral incidents, fluctuating numbers on roll etc. But leaders need to look ahead, attempting predictions of future states to prepare the school for possible changes, or to paint a picture of a future desirable state.

The sense giving competency of navigating the present is challenging because it requires sense giving while the picture is still forming. But it is therefore a good opportunity to help the team to embrace ambiguity and uncertainty. It requires vulnerability but that in turn can help to develop trusting relationships.

Change work is not school improvement in the conventional sense. It is not a programme, a strategy document or an initiative. Change work is architectural. It decides where judgement lives, how risk is carried and which problems the system will stop manufacturing.

If we don't frame the past, we risk leaving successes unattributed and challenges unacknowledged, both of which are crucial to develop institutional memory. If we don't navigate the present, the team will make sense of what is happening and why from multiple, narrow viewpoints and risk fragmented decision making. If we don't inspire the future, we may remain perpetually reactive, leaving us poorly prepared for increasingly challenging times.
The beauty of narrative is that it can provide a structure for sense giving over tenses.

t: The Best Case Fallacy
q: If we always look on the bright side of life then we fall into 'the best case fallacy'. In Scruton's words, this leads inexorably to "a kind of addiction to unreality that informs the most destructive forms of optimism: a desire to cross out reality, as the premise from which practical reason begins, and to replace it with a system of compliant illusions.
Unscrupulous optimism doesn't just distort our private decisions; it shapes public policy, institutional reform and billion dollar procurement programmes.
We routinely launch new policies, spend money on new systems, train teachers in trendy-sounding pedagogical gimmickry and almost never run pilot programmes, or have a clear evaluation plan in place.

Without such an honest and critical appraisal of our efforts we're gambling with children's futures. And the problem with gamblers is that they don't actually see themselves as risk-takers. They convince themselves that they can beat the odds, that they've discovered a fool-proof system to buck the odds.

Judicious pessimism teaches us not to idolise human beings, but to forgive them their faults and to strive in private for their amendments. It teaches us to limit our ambitions in the public sphere, and to keep open the institutions, customs and procedures whereby mistakes are corrected and faults confessed to, rather than aim for some new arrangement in which mistakes are never made.

Complex systems don't fail because individuals behave badly but because ordinary people respond predictably to the incentives the system creates. To hope that everyone will exercise restraint is a wager against human nature, and history suggests it's a very poor bet.

t: The Art of Disagreement
q: And here is what almost every leader gets wrong about disagreement. You were taught to treat it as a process for finding the right answer. In the decisions that matter most, there is often no single right answer available at the moment you must decide, and pretending otherwise is how organisations talk themselves into false confidence.

When two capable, well-informed people reach opposite conclusions from the same evidence, it is usually because the thing itself is uncertain, not because one of them has reasoned badly. The disagreement is a property of the decision, not a defect in the person you are disagreeing with.

If you believe the argument should produce truth, then whoever fails to persuade you is wrong, or obstructive, or protecting something. That is precisely how the STAAR fight turned personal, with each side eventually questioning the other's motives rather than their reasoning.
A board that always votes unanimously is not necessarily aligned. It may simply have learned that dissent is unwelcome, and the cost of that lesson is invisible until something goes badly wrong.

The most dangerous version of dissent is the kind expressed in corridors and side conversations. It carries all the cost of division and none of the benefit, because the decision never gets tested by it.

A well-run disagreement is fast, because it is bounded. The positions are defined, the counter-case is evaluated, the uncertainty is stated, and then somebody decides. What actually slows organisations down is the objection nobody voiced that surfaces three months later, the executive who never really agreed and withholds effort, or the decision that gets relitigated because it was never properly argued the first time.

t: Leadership Lessons from the Tracks
q: The best leaders don’t plan for the ideal scenario; they plan for the realistic one.

Two weeks in close quarters means tension shows up in tone and silence long before it shows up in words. When someone goes quiet at breakfast or when a “I’m fine” has an edge to it. The leaders who keep teams together are the ones who spot this early, not to fix everything, but to notice it’s there.

You don’t build trust with a new team through a mission statement, you build it by solving small, shared problems together. Maybe that’s a missed connection, an unreliable booking, or a “where do we eat now?” Every minor logistical crash is actually a trust-building opportunity in disguise.

The groups who hold their plans loosely tend to have a better time than the ones defending the original spreadsheet at all costs and good leadership is knowing when the plan has served its purpose and when it’s time to evolve it.

The reality is that we can’t control eighteen trains but we can control how we respond when the eighteenth one is cancelled. This is the skill that transfers most directly from work to travel and to pretty much everywhere else: the gap between what happens and how we react is where leadership actually lives.
The groups that come home closer aren’t the ones who never clash, they’re the ones who repair quickly instead of letting it fester into day nine of the silent treatment.

Small celebrations hold a group together more than people realise. A great meal, the view from the train window or that moment when all the preparation came together and saying it out loud matters because teams (and travel groups) run better on shared recognition than they do on gritted-teeth endurance.

None of this is really about travel. It’s about what happens when you put people together who may get on but haven’t been tested by each other yet and then ask them to make a hundred small decisions under mild logistical chaos for two weeks straight. That’s still leadership, it’s just not usually with a rucksack.

t: Are AI Tutors Really Teaching Students — or Just Teaching the Test?
q: Near transfer occurs when learning is applied to a new situation that closely resembles the one in which it was acquired. The underlying structure, environment, and goals are the largely same - only minor details change.

Far transfer occurs when learning is successfully applied to a situation that differs substantially from the original learning context. While the underlying principles remain consistent, the structure, environment, and goals may all have changed.

As any educator can attest, transfer - even relatively near transfer - is one of the greatest challenges in learning. It is remarkably common for students to perform well in one setting yet struggle to apply that same knowledge in another.

This is precisely why (as discussed in our previous post) effective curricula deliberately vary the way students encounter new ideas. Rather than practicing one type of problem repeatedly in one context, students explore the same underlying concept through different modes (writing, speaking, acting), different media (textbooks, whiteboards, flashcards), different environments (the classroom, the laboratory, field trips), and different instructional approaches (explicit instruction, hands-on demonstrations, group discussions).
From Pressey’s teaching machine to brain training to AI tutors, the promise has remained the same: master the program, and that mastery will generalize to the wider world.

The major point here isn’t that students can’t learn from digital tutors – they clearly can. It’s that the learning they produce is often more contextualized, less durable, and less transferable than knowledge developed through more traditional pedagogies. Equally important, where and how we measure learning matters enormously: the closer an assessment resembles the learning environment, the more likely it is to overestimate what students have actually learned.
Put simply, the effectiveness of any digital tutor cannot be separated from the transfer demands of the assessment used to evaluate it.
Ultimately, the true test of learning is not what students can do with the tutor - but what they can still do without it.

q: People naturally learn best from their experiences when they reflect upon them.

these forms of taste do not necessarily feel different from the inside. A calibrated prediction about novice confusion, a lesson that better fits the teacher’s performance, a commitment about the purpose of the subject and a familiar aesthetic all arrive with the same little flash of “no, not like that”. Strong, Gargani and Hacifazlioglu demonstrated the distinction uncomfortably. Experienced educators watched teachers whose value-added effectiveness was already known. The judges agreed reasonably well with one another, but largely failed to identify the teachers whose pupils made greater achievement gains.

Agreement is evidence, but evidence of a narrower kind than we want. It tells us that the preference is shared and reproducible. That may be because teachers have independently learned the same regularity about pupils. But teachers may also agree because they received similar training, inherited the same conventions, hold the same beliefs about good teaching or possess the same professional blind spots. Their errors are unlikely to be independent.

t: Micro-Decisions
q: A micro-decision is the in-the-moment judgement at the heart of responsive teaching. It is the decision to ask one more question instead of moving on, to slow the pace rather than push through the lesson plan, or to revisit an explanation instead of assuming understanding.
their research suggests that teachers make approximately one consequential decision every ninety seconds to two minutes during any given lesson.

Every lesson contains hundreds of these moments. The quality of responsive teaching is determined not by whether teachers make micro-decisions but by how accurately they interpret what is happening in the room before deciding how to proceed.

teachers do not respond directly to classroom events; they respond to the meaning they assign to those events through their mental models. Expert teachers appeared to develop richer, more flexible mental models, enabling them to connect student responses to the wider learning goal, recognise when the evidence no longer matched the plan, and adapt their teaching accordingly.
Understanding develops gradually and often incompletely, and misunderstandings frequently emerge after learning is judged to have taken place.

t: A Letter to Your New Employee
q: When you arrive on time—to work and to meetings—and when you meet your deadlines, you communicate to everyone around you that their time matters. When you don’t, you are telling them the opposite.
I will never ask you to be the most talented person in the room, but I will always expect you to be in the room when the meeting starts.

I ask that you do the work you committed to do at the standard you would want if the roles were reversed. Cutting corners may save you time, but that shortcut will then become one of your colleagues’ problem.
When you visibly care, the people around you try harder. When you visibly don’t, they notice that too.

The ability to absorb criticism without losing your motivation is what separates people who grow from people who plateau. If you can perform under pressure and stay open to correction, there is almost no limit to how far you can go in this organization.

Kestin’s tutor was not a general-purpose chatbot dropped into a physics course. It had the correct solutions in advance, released help one step at a time, required students to attempt work before receiving explanations, and targeted the same material measured by researcher-built pre- and post-tests.

Students liked Khanmigo and saw it as a helpful supplement, but the quantitative result did not show that the AI tutor outperformed the alternatives. That is exactly the pattern districts should care about: engagement and perceived helpfulness can rise without producing a distinctive learning effect.
His claim was not that technology is irrelevant. It was that researchers often confuse the medium with the instructional method delivered through it.

Students who already know how to ask questions, persist through confusion, interpret feedback, and connect examples to underlying concepts are better prepared to benefit from an AI tutor. Students without those habits may need more human structure, not less.

t: The Hidden Curriculum for Adults: Why School Norms Shape Teachers More Than Policies
q: Schools spend enormous amounts of time writing policies that describe how people should behave. Yet, as Doug Lemov argues, norms almost always prove more influential than rules because they shape behaviour beneath conscious awareness. They are “largely invisible and unconscious,” yet often override formal policies because they determine what people come to regard as normal.

In the first, the dominant conversations revolve around workload, difficult pupils and the latest educational initiative that “will all be forgotten by Christmas.” Professional reading is treated with affectionate suspicion. Teachers who leave before five o’clock are jokingly referred to as “part-timers”, while martyrdom enjoys an oddly elevated social status.

If the prevailing norm suggests that asking for help signals weakness, teachers will quietly struggle alone. If staying until seven o’clock becomes synonymous with commitment, workload will expand to fill the available time. If perfectionism becomes the unofficial measure of professionalism, exhaustion slowly acquires the status of virtue.

Rather than repeatedly telling teachers that collaboration matters, make collaboration visible. Rather than encouraging wellbeing, allow respected colleagues to leave at sensible times without apology. Rather than celebrating resilience, celebrate sustainability.

Perhaps that is the most important lesson of all. Every school is constantly teaching its staff what professionalism looks like, whether intentionally or accidentally. The question is not whether norms exist - they always do. The question is whether we are shaping them deliberately or merely inheriting them from the loudest voices in the room.

Social Identity Theory helps explain why these environments diverge so dramatically. Tajfel and Turner (1979) argued that our sense of self is deeply connected to the groups to which we belong. We constantly seek cues about the behaviours that signal membership. The question is rarely, What do I personally believe is best? It is far more often, What do people like me do around here?

Perhaps this also explains why leaders so often struggle to change culture through persuasion alone. We explain the rationale. We share the evidence. We produce beautifully formatted implementation plans. Yet if heuristics guide much of human behaviour automatically, leadership becomes less about convincing people and more about shaping environments in which desirable behaviours become the obvious behaviours.

When experienced teachers openly admit uncertainty, psychological safety begins to grow. Edmondson’s (1999) research demonstrates that teams learn more effectively when individuals feel safe enough to acknowledge mistakes, ask questions and seek feedback without fear of embarrassment. Likewise, Barsade’s (2002) work on emotional contagion reminds us that emotions spread rapidly through organisations. Cynicism is contagious, but luckily, so are optimism, generosity and trust.

t: Stop Chasing Results
q: Most performance problems are visible in behaviour long before they appear in a dashboard. By the time the numbers shift, the habits producing those results are often already firmly established.

Economist Charles Goodhart famously observed that “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”. The moment people are judged solely on a number, they often start optimising the number itself rather than the behaviours that originally produced it.
Ultimately, outcomes tell you whether you succeeded. But it is behaviours that tell you whether you’re likely to succeed again. We should be playing the long game.

More importantly, are you recognising those behaviours when the result wasn’t the one you hoped for? When organisations reward outcomes alone, they risk undervaluing people doing excellent work in difficult circumstances.
Organisations that focus only on performance are essentially measuring history. Organisations that focus on behaviours are shaping the future.

The number wasn’t going to magically change because I stared at it every morning with enough emotional intensity. What I actually needed was habits, structure and consistency. The same applies to organisations.
If someone wanted to earn recognition in your organisation tomorrow, what behaviours would they quickly learn to display? And are those the behaviours you actually want more of?

t: Leaders Who Are Difficult to Shock
q: While many leaders pride themselves on being decisive, some of the best leaders prize being measured. They cultivate a reputation for being difficult to surprise, fluster, or jolt.

When surprised, they pause before answering and do their best to separate their initial emotional reaction from the appropriate organizational response. Over time, they garner a reputation for being hard to rattle and difficult to shock.

Just as visible alarm spreads through an organization and infects morale, visible calm spreads too. When people interact with a leader who refuses to become agitated, flustered, or reactive, they stop bracing and start problem-solving.

Calm leaders make it safer for people to voice views that might be unpopular or controversial. Calm evenness isn’t merely a style. It becomes an information channel, one that keeps hard truths and unpopular opinions flowing upward so leaders can make quality decisions informed by a full range of viewpoints.

Psychologist Sigal Barsade, whose research on emotional contagion in groups helped establish the phenomenon, found that a leader’s mood spreads through a team and shapes how team members think and behave toward one another. Because composed leaders are seen as safe to challenge, they tend to hear more dissenting views and earlier warnings. This is precisely the information leaders need to make good decisions — and the kind of information that anxious teams often suppress.

Leaders who never seem to react, even to good news, risk being perceived as indifferent rather than composed. Good leaders show their emotions, just not reflexively to negative information. If a team scores a huge win and the leader’s expression doesn’t change, the team doesn’t feel steadied.

The best leaders don’t suppress what they feel. They manage the gap between feeling it and showing it. The pause before responding is where composure gets built, one surprise at a time, until it becomes a reputation.

t: Intentional Leadership: How Purpose-Driven Behavior Builds High-Performance Teams
q: In leadership development, few ideas get talked about as much as intention.
But the question that actually shapes how all of that goes often doesn’t get asked: before this conversation, this decision, this whole season of leadership, what are you actually trying to create?

An intention is the internal orientation you bring while you are pursuing that outcome.
It defines not just what you want to accomplish, but who you want to be in the process.
A goal might be to increase team engagement scores by 20% this quarter.
The intention behind that goal might be: I want every person on this team to feel genuinely seen and invested in the work we are doing together.

t: The Power of the Third Turn
q: One question sits behind most of my instructional decisions now: how do I get all of the students thinking more actively, frequently, and deeply about what they're learning?

Every classroom discussion, especially one led by cold call, has three moves: First turn: the teacher’s question. Second turn: the student’s response. Third turn: what the teacher does with that response.

The third turn treats the answer as a starting point of the dialogue. Instead of evaluating and moving on, the teacher uses a follow-up prompt to extend, challenge, clarify, or connect student's thinking, often by handing it to other students.
A first answer is usually only the beginning of understanding and discussion. Students may be able to recall a fact without fully articulating the concept behind it.

the third turn done well creates more opportunities for more students to rehearse their understanding, clarify each other’s thinking, connect concepts, and support their answers with evidence. q: A promotion looks like one reward. It is actually a dozen, welded together and handed over as a unit.

The brain can register a pattern long before it can decompose that pattern into its parts. A person can recognize a friend’s face instantly but struggle to describe it precisely enough that a stranger could pick the friend out of a lineup.

But when quality is missing, something violates your expectations — a hinge that doesn’t close right, a musical note that is flat, a phrase that doesn’t fit. Violated expectations are exactly what perception notices. Attention is drawn to deviation, not confirmation.
No one is explicitly taught the standard for a well-proportioned room. People infer it from having been in hundreds of rooms. This implicit learning is available for judgment but not for explanation.

Being able to say why something is of high quality requires a vocabulary and a standard. Critics, sommeliers, editors, master craftspeople, and skilled facilitators develop this vocabulary specifically so they can articulate what everyone else only feels.
A leader who can recognize quality but can’t teach it can’t scale their standards beyond their own presence. The moment they step out of the room, the standard walks out with them.
Good leaders maintain a focus on quality. Great leaders make it clear where quality comes from and teach it to others.

t: When Does a First Impression Carry Too Much Weight?
q: Two of the most common expressions of this error are the Halo Effect and the Horn Effect; both are forms of what researchers sometimes call 'global impression bias.'
The Halo Effect occurs when one positive trait or experience colors a leader’s expectations across unrelated areas.

People with a halo are viewed as more talented, better at their jobs, and more promotable. They are also likely to be labeled 'high potential,' while equally capable people carrying a horn are systematically underrated, regardless of what their performance data shows.
The hidden danger is that this kind of bias feels like sound judgment rather than distortion. It doesn’t announce itself as a shortcut, so it is seldom questioned in the moment.
Left unchecked, it compounds over time. The person seen favorably keeps getting the benefit of the doubt, while the person viewed unfavorably keeps having to prove themselves from a deficit.
Drawing fast impressions of people is both natural and efficient. But the best leaders don’t allow their first impression to be their last.
good judgment isn’t the absence of bias but rather the discipline of comparing that impression against the evidence that follows.

t: The Proxy Trap
q: Lesson observation, at least as commonly enacted, distorted teaching, pushed teachers to focus on performance rather than learning, and created a system more interested in short-term fluff than real improvement.

if one observer judged a lesson outstanding, the probability that a second observer would give a different grade was between 51% and 78%. If a lesson was judged inadequate, there was a 90% chance that a second observer would grade it differently.
These myths are like bindweed. It's not enough to root them out once, we have to contintually guard against them growing back.
Proxy worship writes policies, designs learning walk protocols, produces book scrutiny pro formas and shapes appraisal targets.
The lesson, then, is that the poor proxies argument has to be turned on itself.
We should always distrust easy inferences but even scepticism can become lazy. We need proxies but we should never rely on them.
The enemy was never engagement, order, feedback, written work or any other visible trace of learning. The enemy has always been our insatiable hunger for easy answers.

The solution is proxy humility: continue observing lessons and checking books, but always distrust easy inferences, recognizing that any single visible trace can be stage-managed.

t: Wellbeing Isn't Cake in the Staff Room. It's Professionalism Done Properly.
q: The teacher who leaves school exhausted every evening doesn't suddenly become well because someone remembered to buy flapjacks. The ECT who is quietly wondering whether they belong in the profession isn't reassured by a fruit bowl.

One of the strongest results showed that teachers who chose to participate in professional development experienced greater wellbeing than those whose participation was mandated. That isn't really about attendance. It's about agency.

This paper also made me wonder whether we have underestimated mentoring as a wellbeing intervention because excellent mentoring reduces uncertainty and builds competence. It replaces anxiety with clarity.

By all means, keep the cake. Just don't mistake it for the foundations. The foundations are much more substantial than that. They are built through excellent mentoring, thoughtful leadership, purposeful professional development and a culture that takes people's professional growth seriously.

The reason so many managers struggle is not that they lack intelligence or effort. It’s that management is a craft that must be honed over many years, but we treat it like a promotion that occurs overnight.

The skills that made them successful in their previous role are no longer the skills that determine their success going forward. Yet in many organizations, there is little or no formal preparation for this transition.

There are certainly pieces of it that can be learned “academically” — frameworks, research studies, and principles that can help. But the actual practice of leadership is learned through repetition, coaching, observation, reflection, and feedback.
These are not skills most people magically acquire because they were good at their previous job and got promoted. So, the result is that many people become bad managers when they get that promotion.

The reason is usually the irrational fear that if they invest in training, people might leave and take that training with them to another company. Or that if they help people grow, they will ask for promotions or raises.

The Catch-22 One statistic captures the problem perfectly: Roughly 70% of people who leave a job do so because of some form of conflict or dissatisfaction with their manager. Many organizations are basically creating this scenario for themselves.

t: Texas Has a Theory of Education
q: This June, the Texas State Board of Education adopted [ ] new social studies standards and a required literature reading list for its public schools. These changes follow Texas’s 2024 release [ ] of its “Bluebonnet” curriculum, a package of instructional resources for elementary school, which sparked controversy over the inclusion of Bible stories in the reading materials.

The standards explicitly call for concepts to be embedded in stories and historical content in order to “create schema for understanding.” This is a significant departure from the way American education often thinks about social studies—and education more broadly. For decades, schools have been encouraged to focus on skills: critical thinking, problem solving, analysis, collaboration, and, in literacy, comprehension strategies such as finding the main idea, making inferences, and identifying the author’s purpose.

A school system cannot be indifferent to whether one classroom studies ancient Egypt, another spends six weeks on a generic unit about “communities,” and a third pursues student-selected projects, and then assume all children will arrive at the next grade equally prepared. It should not be controversial for them to cultivate some measure of affection for the community, state, and country that created and sustains them. This need not require triumphalism, mythology, or silence about injustice.

The Texas social studies standards are admirably explicit about this knowledge-building component of civics. They aim to develop responsible citizens who understand constitutional government, consent of the governed, civic virtue, individual rights, and the preservation of liberty.

t: Overcoming Animosity Toward a Team Member
q: Without necessarily meaning to, leaders sometimes hold a grudge. They can let their negative impressions and feelings toward a team member influence how they engage with them.
The good news is that fixing it doesn’t require the team member to change at all. Animosity is a deep-seated dislike or resentment toward another person.
Learning how to overcome this feeling is essential to effective leadership. The first is a discrete event where the leader feels deeply wronged, betrayed, deceived, humiliated, or rejected.

Much more commonly, leaders feel animosity because of psychological, ideological, and value differences between themselves and their team members — differences perceived as a threat, no matter how exaggerated, irrational, or mistaken that perception turns out to be. In those cases, the animosity is less about what actually happened than about what the leader believes it to mean.

Each unpleasant exchange makes the next one easier to read as further proof of the other person’s flaws, until the leader is no longer responding to what the team member actually did but to an accumulated impression of who they are. Psychologists call this negative sentiment override, and once it takes hold, even neutral or well-intentioned behavior gets filtered through that lens.

Leaders will likely find some of the actions and behaviors of their team members annoying or irritating at times. But what commonly turns ordinary annoyance into animosity isn’t the behavior or its repetition, but the interpretation the leader assigns to it.

This means it can be addressed by changing how the leader interprets the behavior, independent of whether the team member changes anything at all. Leaders who want to overcome their animosity must learn to stop interpreting a team member’s actions as intentionally harmful and personally aimed at them.
x: The starting point for resolution is accepting that the team member does not need to change — the leader's task is to change their own interpretive frame, which is something the leader has complete agency over.

t: A Letter to a Young Head of Department
q: Over the past few months I’ve had a series of increasingly depressing series of encounters with heads of English seeking on advice and guidance on how to contend with senior leaders who seem intent on making their lives as hard as possible. The following letter represents both my frustration and despair as well as a repository of all the pearls of wisdom I’ve tried to share.

By serious, I don’t mean solemn — solemnity is frequently the counterfeit of thought — I mean that you must preserve an allegiance to reality. Line managers may prefer a fog of intentions, but you need to develop a taste for facts.

Better to say, “Last time we met, we agreed that behaviour support would be arranged before the end of the week. That hasn’t happened, so I need to know whether the support is still coming or whether I’m expected to manage this without it.” Separate motive from effect.

People do struggle, and humane leadership requires more than pointing at standards and relying on shame. But standards must always remain visible, otherwise support becomes a place to hide rather than a route back to doing the job properly.

But, as you well know, a lesson isn’t good because it comes on a slide deck packaged with approved ‘dual coded’ logos but because it causes students to know something worth knowing or do something worth doing. Architecture that enables this is useful anything that prevents it is an obstacle course arranged in front of a fire exit.

We all wanted to be trusted but to be trustworthy you must be honest. Over committing — promising what you’d like to happen but which you know is unrealistic — is always worse than disappointing people at the outset.
Compromise can be a form of cowardice but, when intelligently chosen, it’s not surrender. Of course, your school is not a salon convened for the satisfaction of your ideals.

t: Designing a Predictive Talent Index Based on Your Best People
q: To evaluate and select talent, organizations naturally rely on personality assessments and psychological diagnostics to learn more about people. By digging deeper into the motivations, tendencies, and styles of prospective candidates and those up for promotion, leaders gain the data and confidence they need to make better choices.

As general predictors of how people will show up and behave once in a position, these assessments add a lot of value, which is one reason they are so popular. Because good leaders treat assessment results as another data point and not as a litmus test for selection, it is not uncommon for organizations to use multiple diagnostics at the same time.

But the best leaders and organizations have learned to take the fullest advantage of these assessments by using them more strategically. Leaders naturally want a true predictive tool to make their selections more accurate, so they turn to their best people to create one.

Finding a common pattern of that success can be a huge advantage in the selection process. The best leaders ask their top people to complete as many diagnostics and assessments as possible until a pattern correlated with success emerges.

For example, if an organization relies on the DISC assessment to test for features of personality, applying this tool to the best performers may reveal a pattern that can be used for prediction. If nearly all the organization’s top performers share a common set of personality results (in DISC, let’s say they are all High Ds and Cs), that pattern can now be used to find others with the same orientation.

Organizations can spend several years with a large set of assessment tools before they land on a pattern they have confidence in. But once they concoct that magic potion, it can significantly improve their selection process.
Organizations that do the work end up with more than a predictive tool. They create a mirror of what success in personality and style actually looks like in their culture.

t: The Science of Reading in High School: Engaging Rhetorical Exemplars in the ELA Classroom
q: In contemporary public discourse, it’s clear that many people have not been taught how to argue effectively. Name-calling, groundless accusations, guilt by association, and other logical fallacies are sprinkled throughout the news, social media, and conversations.

Each semester, I thought of this unit as my small attempt to address this broader problem by at least introducing the students in my class to a better way. The core of the unit was the pairing of two seminal rhetorical texts: “Letter to Viceroy, Lord Irwin” by Mohandas Gandhi [ ] and “Letter from a Birmingham Jail” by Dr.

I would begin the unit with Gandhi’s letter, since it preceded King and served as an inspiration for his nonviolent direct action during the Civil Rights Movement. After guiding my students through a close reading of the text and developing a summary paragraph, I would direct their attention to the rhetorical devices for a second look at the text using a jigsaw activity.

Following this, I would call on members from each group to share an example of each rhetorical device, and I would restate and clarify the way each example demonstrated an effective use of rhetoric. Lastly, after our whole class discussion, students would complete a SOAPSTone analysis chart and paragraph to synthesize their thinking about Gandhi’s message and his use of rhetoric.

First, given the length of the letter, I would strategically scaffold the reading of the text. To start, I would set our expectations and direct students to look for and annotate certain elements in King’s prose.

Finally, I would have students write a gist or summary statement for the first eleven paragraphs. This prepares students to engage in a similar routine that they will complete in groups as we jigsawed the remaining paragraphs of the letter.

Lastly, one element of their assessment over this unit was a written comparison of the use of rhetoric in the two texts. This assignment helps students demonstrate their analysis and argumentation skills, their ability to cite and interpret text evidence, and practice synthesizing information from two separate sources.

t: Nonexperts Use the Wrong Criteria to Make Selections of Quality
q: Many of an organization’s worst decisions aren’t made by incompetent people. They are made by smart, confident people who are nonexperts in the domain where they have decision-making authority.

They don’t decide wrongly because they ignore important criteria but because they give too much weight to superficial attributes, such as brand, social proof, and likeability, and too little weight to the performance criteria most important to true experts. Research reveals that nonexperts also prioritize immediate outcomes, such as short-term comfort and speed of implementation, over long-term effectiveness, established track record, and strategic fit.

Instead of asking, “Is this program or vendor good?” they ask, “Does this feel right to me?” They know that feeling right is much easier to defend in a meeting than being right. This is one reason so many low-quality programs, experts, and experiences are brought into organizations and become deeply entrenched over years.

For instance, when marketing experts make artistic decisions, or when human resources experts decide between artificial intelligence tools, they depend too heavily on what others are doing rather than doing the work to discern quality and performance. Busy leaders make the same poor decisions when they stray from their core expertise.

Of course, this leads to poor choices across any domain where they lack true expertise. Nonexperts are drawn to cues that are easy to interpret, like brand familiarity, visual polish, or social media reviews.

So, brand familiarity, visual polish, and social media reviews crowd out more objective measures of quality when they make decisions regarding which programs, people, and tools to bring into the organization. Over time, these weak choices can have a tremendously negative impact on the overall quality of the organization.

The tragedy is that it feels indistinguishable from good judgment to the person exercising it. A confident choice predicated on superficial criteria carries all the emotional weight of a well-reasoned one, which is precisely what makes it so dangerous.

Thinking, “This lesson is not that difficult, so there is no reason students should be confused,” creates emotional distance between the teacher and the learning—or lack of learning—happening in the classroom. If a lesson is not that difficult, then it must be the student’s fault for not understanding.

Veteran teachers will have taught some topics hundreds of times, and this level of subject consistency has many benefits. It allows us to use previously created materials and to fine-tune them throughout the years.

No matter how badly I want to be good at chess, I cannot seem to improve to a level I find satisfactory. Even when I do feel myself beginning to improve, this always seems to be followed by a demoralizing losing streak.

There have been times when I became so angry after a series of losses that I’ve had to force myself to give up chess for weeks at a time. Every week, they are forced to spend time wallowing in their aggravation.

Just because it is easy for us after the hundredth time does not mean it will be easy for our students on their first try. It is our job to be compassionate and patient and to find a way to reach our struggling students.
I admit that it hurt to hear these students didn’t understand the material. I could have let myself think, “Why are students still having trouble with this topic?

t: AI in Education #12: Five Things I Learned from Zach Groshell about What's Actually Inside the Alpha School Maths Apps
q: Zach could ask Claude to teach adding 4 + 3, take what it gives, ask for it “a different way”, and deploy the result. Instead, he does the opposite. He digs into the actual Engelmann programs, reads, copies and edits the material by hand, and only once he has it right in his head does he hand the assembly to the AI.

The early assumption was that the technology people could generate the lessons themselves - they had the tools, they could make it slick and bug-free. It failed straight away. You need the domain experts in the loop. Engelmann knew this decades ago, which is why he paired his instructional-design brain with subject-matter experts in history, science and maths.

The child rarely watches for more than about 9 seconds before they have to respond. The steps are tiny. Several strands run in parallel and get chained together, typically across three exposures over three days, before a timed mastery test. Roughly 90% of any lesson is review; only about 10% is the new, slightly harder thing. As Zach put it, it is cognitive load theory in a bottle.

A lot of retrieval, Zach argues - especially in maths - is what he bluntly calls dumb retrieval. We pick a small skill, decide it is “a thing”, and dutifully space it out across the whole year on an ever-expanding interval. But if a child is now doing column addition, identifying the digits and setting out the problem, is already baked into the task.

Zach chose Montessorium for his daughter. Not because he doubts the apps - he builds them - but because she loves reading whole books, journaling and drawing, and the sport-in-the-afternoon model would do nothing for her. The apps, in other words, are not a school.

t: The Catcher in the Rye and the Classroom Moment
q: In the last few years I have started two book clubs, both of which have added a little direction and purpose to my leisure reading. One of those clubs began as a philosophy reading club with a half-dozen members, but coordinating the schedules of six or seven people for video discussions is definitely not one of my life skills, so it kind of petered out.

In May we read Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet [ ], and last month we had a great discussion of The Catcher in the Rye [ ]. I don’t remember when I first read Salinger’s novel, but it was probably in high school.

And what would never have been clear to me as a young reader was flashing like a siren through every page: this is a 16-year-old child who has been traumatized by the death of his brother, and no adult in his life seems to acknowledge how deeply it has affected him, or offer him any real help. His parents never appear in the novel, except in brief references, none of which present them in a positive light.

I know, that’s 2026 talking, and we should consider the novel in its historical context. And, indeed, eventually our book club discussion did move beyond our analysis of Holden’s mental state into the final scene in the penultimate chapter of the novel.

The final chapter, just a page and a half long, describes him in some kind of institutionalized setting a year later, under the care of psychoanalysts, wondering what will become of him. (That seems to be Salinger’s warning that Holden has gone too far in rejecting all of society’s conventions.) But the scene with Phoebe on the carousel, at least to an English professor like me, screams out for analysis.

I want you to read silently that page of the novel again, and then take out a half-sheet of paper and write me one full paragraph explaining what you think makes Holden happy in that moment. What’s different for that Holden in that scene?” After ten minutes of writing, I would have asked for volunteeers, and then began writing possible interpretations on the board.

I know this both from talking to faculty and observing them in the classroom. These teachers seek for their students what Holden seeks for himself and finds in the scene with Phoebe: a few moments of presence, authentic connections with other humans, a recognition of something meaningful in process.

t: The 3-Step Framework That Makes Impromptu Speeches Actually Survivable
q: Why impromptu speeches feel harder than they should There is a specific kind of dread that comes with being called on to speak without warning. It is not the same as stage fright, and it is not the same as presentation nerves.

They are running a small, repeatable process that removes most of the panic from the moment. What follows is that process, distilled into three simple steps — Inquire, Research, Build — plus the practical advice that ties them together.

Step 1 — Inquire The first move happens days before the impromptu moment ever arrives. Ask your professor, your manager, your event organizer — whoever is running the setting — what kinds of questions or prompts you should expect.

Some will refuse to tell you anything specific, which is itself useful information — it tells you the moment will be genuinely open-ended and you should prepare more broadly. They assume the impromptu nature of the exercise means preparation is impossible.

Step 2 — Research Once you know the rough shape of what might come up, the next move is preparation — but not the kind most people think of. It matters that you are informed on recent social issues — climate change, current events, the topics that show up in serious conversation right now — and that you understand the background well enough to speak from a real perspective rather than from vague opinion.
With good preparation, three minutes is enough time to structure a coherent impromptu response. There is an optional layer here that most people skip, and it is worth adding: light rehearsal.
Where the article ends for free readers The first two steps — Inquire and Research — build the foundation. They shrink the unknown and give you real material to draw from.

t: Research Bite #72: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
q: Phone restrictions in schools are spreading fast, but hard evidence has been thin. This US study evaluates one stringent version: lockable pouches (the Yondr brand) that students seal their phones into for the whole school day.

Using nationwide data on middle and high schools and a staggered difference-in-differences design, the researchers combined GPS phone signals, standardised test scores, attendance, discipline records and student surveys.
Adopting pouches sharply cut in-school phone use, with teachers reporting personal phone use in class falling from 61% to 13%.
Yet the wider effects were modest. Disciplinary incidents rose and student well-being dipped in the first year, then well-being turned positive and discipline settled.
Average test scores barely moved, with small gains in high school maths offset by small dips in middle schools. Attendance and bullying were unaffected.

q: For the reasonable price of just $5 AUD per month or $50 per year, you can be a full subscriber to Filling the Pail with complete access to my extensive archive on a range of topics, as well as access to the unabridged version of my weekly Curios posts. I am a long-term sceptic of ‘differentiation’ or ‘differentiated instruction’.
That would seem to fix the problem of planning many different tasks, while also allowing for differentiation. Students could be grouped within the class and tackle the task differently.

This is because problem solving taxes mental resources to the extent that there is often no attention left over to notice patterns. Instead, if we want students to learn mathematics, a planned, sequenced approach where concepts are explicitly introduced would seem to be a better bet [ ].
I am therefore not sure exactly what mathematics this is targeting. The prompt mentions students ‘may construct models using dynamic geometric software and apply trigonometry’.

Unfortunately, I can see it keeping students busy for an extended period of time and I worry that may be the attraction. What is clear is that despite the framing, these tasks are cover for a form of inquiry learning.

This is a highly significant constraint and is essentially the same constraint as a low floor/threshold. Kapur managed this constraint in some of his work by focusing on standard deviation and asking which baseball player was the most consistent.

Low floor high ceiling tasks therefore are a form of inquiry learning, but they are an impoverished form even of inquiry learning. Worse, they are designed to generate busywork and activity that looks like students are doing mathematics when they are not learning anything much at all.

q: A recent chapter by Joellen Killion in the Third International Handbook of Educational Change highlights deliberate practice as one of the defining features of effective instructional coaching. Alongside goal setting, modelling and feedback, deliberate practice enables teachers to translate professional learning into improved classroom practice.
Twenty years of driving does not automatically make someone an expert driver. It often means one year of experience repeated twenty times. Teaching can be similar.

La Trobe University's practice labs represent an impressive investment in this approach. They provide environments where pre-service teachers can rehearse core teaching practices before, during and alongside their professional placements.
Confidence is often assumed to emerge naturally with experience. In reality, confidence grows when people repeatedly experience success performing challenging tasks.

The same coaching cycle of goal setting, modelling, feedback, rehearsal and reflection remains valuable whether someone has taught for one year or thirty. Professional learning therefore becomes an ongoing process rather than an occasional workshop.

t: All Cultures Are Local
q: But the culture that team members actually experience is shaped most strongly by their immediate environment, not by the organization's corporate culture.

Culture is the stable, organization-wide set of values and norms that shape meaning and experience. Climate is the local weather system a team lives inside day to day, shaped almost entirely by its leader and colleagues.
Managers across the globe account for at least 70% of the variance in team engagement.
One weak leader who allows communication to become fragmented and relationships to become transactional can ruin the experience of everyone on the team.
Culture isn’t declared at the enterprise level. It is built one team, one leader, and one conversation at a time.

t: When Words Kill: How Institutions Govern a World That No Longer Exists
q: In October 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 crashed into the Java Sea twelve minutes after takeoff. Five months later, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 went down under almost identical circumstances.

This is not a story about negligence or fraud, though those questions have been litigated elsewhere. It is a story about something more structural, and in some ways more disturbing: the way institutional language can become decoupled from the reality it purports to govern, invisibly, gradually, and with catastrophic consequences.

That inheritance has real advantages: stable language is enforceable, legally defensible, professionally coherent. Those advantages create genuine resistance to revision, even when revision is obviously needed.

But the signals reinforcing stable language are dense and immediate, every successful certification milestone, every training classification that holds, while the signals that would motivate revision are diffuse, delayed, and filtered before they reach anyone with authority to act. Boeing’s oversight was almost entirely conducted after certification, not before.

When reality reasserted itself, $1.9 trillion in mortgage-backed securities were downgraded in a matter of months. The post-crisis fix was revealing: regulators introduced a new suffix, “(sf),” to distinguish structured finance ratings from corporate ones.

The words available to them encoded assumptions about authorship and misconduct that generative AI had rendered structurally inapplicable, and because those words were canonical, professionally reproduced, and legally embedded, they persisted. Why This Matters ISD is not an argument that institutions are stupid or corrupt.
That’s why it looks like a crash, a crisis, a cliff, rather than a gradual recalibration. By the time the gap between language and reality is undeniable, the gap is enormous.
