t: The Story Is Not Always Yours to Write
q: When Serena Williams announced she was returning to competitive tennis after nearly four years away, everyone had a theory. At 44, walking back onto courts where 20-year-olds now roam, Serena knew the verdicts would come from every direction.

Asked about the fanfare surrounding her return, she offered one of the most instructive answers of her career: It’s not up to her what others make of it. So she stated her reasons plainly — she wanted her daughters to see her play.

This week, Serena walked off Centre Court to a standing ovation, having taken a set from a player half her age, her daughters cheering from the front row. The loss on the scoreboard didn’t touch the win she came for.

Many leaders, especially those with high global or local visibility, operate differently. They exhaust themselves managing perception, pre-spinning decisions, over-explaining, chasing down every critic.
They delay hard calls while imagining how the announcement will land. All that energy spent on the narrative is energy not spent on the work.

People judge leaders by what they repeatedly do, not by what they say about what they do. Good leaders define what they do with clear reasons, state them once, and let their consistency do the explaining.
When misunderstood, they check whether their behavior needs to change. They spend their energy where it compounds: on standards, on preparation, on the people in front of them.

t: The Paradox of Value-Added Measures in Schools
q: One of the enduring challenges in education is deciding how we know whether a school has made a difference. Schools admit students with different levels of prior attainment, different experiences, different opportunities and different challenges.

For schools educating comprehensive or genuinely mixed-ability cohorts, this matters enormously. It offers a way of demonstrating impact that is fairer than raw attainment alone, and for that reason it has become one of the most influential measures of school effectiveness in many educational contexts.

What strikes me now, however, is not what the diagram includes. By separating these influences into distinct contributors, I implicitly suggested that they could be considered independently of one another.
Over the years, I have occasionally found that talking about context is interpreted as making excuses. High expectations and developmental understanding are not competing philosophies.

Neural pathways that are used repeatedly become increasingly efficient through myelination, whilst others are pruned away. t: How Many Types of Thinking Are There?
q: Robert Epstein’s widely cited argument [ ] has convinced thousands of people that the computer metaphor for the brain is wrong on several fronts. The brain has no software, no algorithms, and no manufactured processors.
Why do we so readily believe that language machines can think? If the brain is not a computer processing a single type of 'data,' then the ways we interact with the world must be equally varied.

No one can experiment on the past, only reconstruct it from what survived, which makes it an exercise in inference under permanent incompleteness. Political and civic reasoning add a constraint neither science nor ethics requires alone: the answer has to be reached with other people who don’t always share premises.

Its first criterion isn’t about the world at all but about the reasoner. Capstone-level “Ethical Self-Awareness” requires a student to discuss in detail both their core beliefs and the origins of those beliefs with depth and clarity.

Scientific thinking is vulnerable to plausibility bias — evaluating evidence by assessing the plausibility of a hypothesized cause, making judgments about the world in ways that are consistent with prior belief — precisely because it’s in constant contact with a messy empirical world that admits of prior expectation. Mathematical thinking has no analogous contamination risk, because it isn’t testing a claim against nature; it’s testing a claim against a closed deductive system.

Creative thinking and magical thinking share surface features. Both traffic in the impossible, the counterfactual, the not-yet-real — and diverge completely on what happens to that material afterward.

Creative thinking asks what else might be possible and then puts the possibility to work; magical thinking picks the possibility up and holds onto it, even when it doesn’t work. None of them are lesser or better versions of “thinking in general.” They are easy to conflate by teaching critical thinking, for example, as if it includes ethical reason, too, or “STEM thinking” as if math and science are one skill.

t: Children of the Magenta Line
q: In 1997, American Airlines captain Warren VanderBurgh gave a lecture warning about the dangers of autopilot [ ]. He titled it "children of the magenta line," after the magenta coloured course line the flight computer draws across a cockpit display.

This is what schema theorists have in mind when they talk about assimilation of knowledge and say we grasp a new thing only by fastening it to things we already hold: the richer the existing weave, the more points at which a new thread can catch. This is why knowledge doesn’t just add to what you know but also compounds what you are able to learn next, and why the child with the fuller store of knowledge pulls further ahead with every passing year.

Phil Christman, who teaches first-year writing, comes closest in Slate [ ]: the chatbot, he grants, “hurts their ability to learn”, but the deeper casualty he says is “the trust that any teaching relationship depends on”. He is right that trust is a casualty, and he is not alone in his unease; a New Yorker essay by Jessica Winter [ ]recently conveyed the turning tide, “a growing number of parents, educators, and cognitive scientists” now saying that AI does not belong in the rooms where children learn.

Why Minimally Guided AI Does Not Work In 2006 Paul Kirschner , John Sweller and Richard Clark published a paper which had a huge influence on me and many other educators based in the UK : Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work [ ]. Their target was the whole family of “minimally guided” approaches such as discovery learning, problem-based learning, inquiry learning, constructivism, that broadly share a single misguided idea: that learners build knowledge most durably when they construct it for themselves rather than being shown explicitly.

The key idea here for me is that memorisation is fast and cheap; generalisation is slow, and arrives late if it arrives at all, and on some tasks never comes, because the data stays, in the researchers’ own phrase, effectively random to the model. In other words, the network prefers the patterns that are quick to learn and poor at transferring, and only reluctantly gives them up for the slow ones that actually generalise.

It follows the same stubborn principles either way: mastery before moving on, effortful retrieval, the right cognitive load at the right moment. I also realised that almost everything I learned since the age of 12, I have learned on my own.

But what we have so rarely solved is how to give thirty children at thirty different points all of that at once, from one teacher, in one room, for one hour. The best teachers approximate it through sheer virtuosity, craft and stamina, and often burn out doing so.

t: It's the Instructional Design, Stupid
q: In 1983, Richard Clark asked the field to consider a grocery truck. Media (i.e., technology), he argued, are “mere vehicles that deliver instruction but do not influence student achievement any more than the truck that delivers our groceries causes changes in our nutrition.” The truck matters for cost and reach.

Again and again, people seem to care more about the carrier they can see than the design they cannot. Robert Kozma’s 1994 reply made the argument that particular media have particular capabilities — the symbol systems they can employ, and the operations they can perform on those symbols: displaying, storing, transforming, responding — and that these capabilities, together with the methods that employ them, interact with the cognitive and social processes by which learners construct knowledge.

If Clark is right, the medium is beside the point — a computer can deliver instruction just as a teacher can, provided the design is sound. If Kozma is right, the medium matters, but only in this sense: its capabilities must be able to execute the method.

It is there to be used and extended, and almost nobody has.¹ Theory of Instruction (Engelmann & Carnine, 1982) is not a book about teacher behaviors. It is a logical analysis of communication: how to construct a sequence of examples and non-examples that admits exactly one interpretation, so that the learner cannot induce a misrule no matter what irrelevant features happen to co-occur.

They were brilliant adaptations to the capabilities and limits of the classroom-as-medium. Enter the app, which doesn’t need the workarounds: it attends to each learner individually rather than rounding up to the group, never tires of the script, never feels micromanaged by it, and delivers it exactly, every time, to every child.

But a machine that adheres to a Theory of Instruction analysis will not only teach well — it can place each learner at the right entry point, catch and correct every error the moment it’s made, and enforce a mastery criterion with a consistency that’s structurally impossible in a class of 30. Redrawing the lines When people say a computer can’t deliver instruction, they have observed — correctly — that almost all educational software is bad.

If two vehicles can carry the method to the same criterion, and one of them can reach children the other never will, then choosing it isn’t icky. So yes, the lines are being redrawn — and not only in online debates.

t: Happy Birthday America: 250 Years of Unlimited Debate
q: We spend the school year cataloguing everything wrong with American education, often correctly. Summer is the season to notice what is right with it: thousands of kids choosing, on their own vacation, to think harder than school requires, about the most consequential questions in the country, under an obligation to understand the people they disagree with.

The preliminary vote was so fragile that Congress postponed the final decision a day so wavering delegations could come around. Dickinson lost the argument, and knowing his vote could wreck the unanimity the moment required, he stayed away from the chamber so the decision would carry the full weight of the whole.

Then the entire country got to argue about whether to accept it. The ratification fight of 1787–88 was a national debate conducted in newsprint — eighty-five essays [ ] by “Publius” on one side, a barrage of Anti-Federalist replies on the other, with thirteen state conventions sitting as the judges.

Lincoln lost the Senate seat and won the argument; he published the debates as a book, and two years later the argument made him president. Hold that format in your mind — three hours, standing, on the most explosive question in American life — the next time someone with a mute button and a sixty-second shot clock tells you you’re watching a “debate.” The tradition held long enough to pass the hardest test the twentieth century gave it.

It is the precise instant the American system failed — force substituted for rebuttal — and admirers across the South mailed Brooks replacement canes [ ] to congratulate him. Five years later came the war, and roughly 750,000 dead [ ] settled a question that Congress had first refused to debate and then proved unable to.

And at this moment, that question is being settled the way the gag-rule Congress settled slavery: by not arguing it. The real decisions are made by default — by release schedules, capital expenditure, and competitive pressure — while public argument gets waved off from one side as doomer hysteria and from the other as Luddite cope.

Summer is the season to notice what is right with it: thousands of kids choosing, on their own vacation, to think harder than school requires, about the most consequential questions in the country, under an obligation to understand the people they disagree with. Two crises, one answer Both of the institutions this essay loves are in real trouble, and everyone knows it.

t: Why I Hate Beautiful Books
q: An exercise book is so temptingly inspectable. It sits there, solid and available, full of dates, titles, diagrams, worksheets, corrections, and comments in variously coloured pens. You can pick it up, flick through it and feel you’ve seen something.

They tell us what to notice before we’ve had a chance to think. If there’s a box to tick about marking frequency, coloured pens, written responses, presentation or evidence of progress, what matters has been pre-determined. The best we can hope to find is what we were looking for in the first place.

Pride” isn’t equally easy for every student to display in the approved form. For some, neatness is cheap: they can write quickly, organise space, copy accurately and still attend to the explanation. For others, the same requirements consume the working memory we’d rather they spent on the subject.

If the lesson ends with everyone having copied the teacher’s answer, the most important part of the sequence has probably been skipped. The “we do” phase should involve students making decisions with support, and the “you do” phase should require them to attempt something independently. Copying a sentence prompt, or a paragraph plan can help prepare students for independent work, but it can’t replace it.

This is especially damaging when students are asked to write at length before they know enough to write well. They fill pages with clumsy sentences, vague claims, weak evidence, bolted-on quotations and half-formed explanations. The result may look like effort, but it can easily become rehearsal in doing the wrong thing.

Before we argue about whether exercise books should be beautiful, we need to ask a simpler question: what are they for? The answer’s less obvious than it seems because schools often expect books to do several incompatible jobs. In a single subject they may be a place to think, a record of practice, a revision resource and evidence for accountability purposes.

In March, a jury in California found Meta and Google, which owns YouTube, liable for harming children. t: Wait Time
q: Tom noted that, if the goal is to be totally unambiguous through nomenclature, the pause and the crucial thinking time would be in the name itself, and suggested “Question, Pause, Name” as an alternative.

Wait time is not an easy strategy. I know this from personal experience. I like pace in my lessons, and I worked hard over the years at removing dead time... I think a by-product of that is that wait time got forgotten.

Even so, wait time combined with name-end questioning is, in my opinion, one of the most inclusive things a teacher can use in the classroom. It is telling students: your thoughts matter. All of your thoughts matter. I value your thinking.

t: From Protein Chips to EdTech
q: There are two multi-billion-dollar industries in America, and they share a lot in common. Both are quick to jump on the latest trends, both easily convince their “customers” that the evidence is undeniable, and both insist that those trends saturate every aspect of the industry. The two entities I’m referring to are the diet and weight-loss industry and the K-12 education industry.

Much like the cyclical nature of weight-loss fads, both entities have become fixated on peddling the latest breakthrough rather than adhering to foundational practices supported by decades of clear evidence. They frequently mistake novelty for genuine progress, leaving both “customers” and students to bear the ultimate cost.

It wasn’t the exorbitant amount of money spent or the lack of significant improvement that alerted me to the similarities between the diet-and-weight-loss industry and the education industry. It was actually a teacher friend who posted a picture of a protein-infused bag of chips. A high-protein diet is the latest weight-loss trend, so, naturally, everything from chips to water now contains excessive amounts of this magic ingredient that promises to satisfy hunger and build muscle.

Education has experienced a similar impulse: the belief that technology should be woven into nearly every aspect of teaching and learning. Initially, the education community celebrated computers and other technologies for the way they promised to simplify and streamline teachers’ tasks. The same community embraced educational technology for the way it got students excited about learning.

Unfortunately, in recent years, this has morphed into some teachers being unable to do their jobs effectively without the assistance of technology, and many students refusing to engage when they consider the task or assignment “boring”. It has also led to reduced learning due to the passive nature of most educational technology.

In other words, just as the fad diets weren’t inherently bad in themselves, technology in schools is not necessarily bad. How it’s used, how much schools rely on it to solve all their problems, and whether or not the technology is moving the needle on student learning are the real issues. After investing roughly $30 billion in educational technology in 2024, schools have little evidence that those expenditures produced meaningful gains in student achievement.

t: Leading Team Members Who Start Out Strong But Fizzle Out Over Time
q: Team members who start out strong, demonstrate their skills through results, and appear to settle comfortably into the culture are a big win for leaders. But over time, these capable people sometimes lose their momentum, begin to underperform, and seem very different from the persona they projected early on.

Leading team members who begin powerfully but fizzle out over time is both highly disappointing and a unique challenge for leaders. There are many reasons a team member’s performance can drop off a cliff after a couple of years of strong results — some preventable, others coachable, and a few that may well be unchangeable.
The first task of the leader is to generate a theory as to why. Exploring this reality, no matter how uncomfortable it might be for both parties, is the place to start formulating an explanation.

Among the most common explanations for this performance arc is a mismatch between the role and the person’s evolving ambitions. People grow, and what once excited and challenged the team member may no longer hold the same appeal.

When the role remains static even as the person develops new interests, stronger skills, or broader aspirations, disengagement becomes almost inevitable. Leaders who surface this possibility early often discover that a modest adjustment in responsibilities, scope, or opportunity is all that is needed to reignite the energy and output that once defined the team member’s contribution.

A second and more difficult explanation involves the team member’s relationship with the organization itself. Sometimes what fizzles is not the person’s competence but their confidence in leadership, their belief in the mission, or their trust in the culture they once embraced.

It is rarely announced and easily mistaken for laziness or indifference. Sometimes the disengagement can be rectified by exploring why they have come to believe what they do and advocating for a different frame or interpretation of the events and incidents that created their distrust.

q: The most important question for a senior leader is not, 'What did I see?' but, 'Where is the system least aligned?'
A compliance culture asks whether learning walks have happened, whether data has been entered and whether meetings have taken place. An improvement culture asks what those activities changed.

Cold calling is not effective because it is visible during an observation. It is effective when it increases thinking, makes participation more equitable and helps the teacher gather information about understanding.

If Year 10 outcomes in a subject are weaker than expected, leaders should resist jumping straight to more monitoring or more intervention. They might instead ask whether pupils are failing to remember core knowledge.
The loop is not complete when evidence has been collected. It is complete when teaching changes and pupils know, remember or can do more.

t: Faded Scaffolding: Keeping Challenge High While Building Independence
q: A scaffold is successful when it becomes less necessary. The danger is not the scaffold itself, but the permanent scaffold: the support that stays so long pupils learn to complete the prompt rather than think, write, read or solve independently.
If the task is too easy, the scaffold is unnecessary. If the task has been simplified until pupils no longer meet the core demand, support has slipped into low expectations.

Fading is not a sudden jump from full support to no support. It is a series of professional decisions based on evidence of readiness. The question is not, Have I used a scaffold? but, What information tells me that this scaffold can now be reduced, narrowed or removed?

One mutation is the permanent crutch, where the support stays forever and pupils learn the routine rather than the strategy. Another is the worksheet mutation, where scaffolding becomes extra paper rather than better modelling, questioning or checking.
Faded scaffolding is not about doing less for pupils. It is about using the right support at the right time, then reducing it when evidence shows they are ready.

t: Behind Every Great School
q: Summer is a time for reflection for me, and lately the need for great leadership in schools has been at the top of my mind. So this post is for the leaders who made me, and every teacher they’ve worked with, a better teacher.

She had a clear vision, clear expectations for what good teaching looked like, clear standards for what kids should be doing and learning. But, and this is the part so many leaders miss, she backed those expectations with the time, support and tools to meet them.
She had promised to balance classrooms if I stayed in 4th instead of moving down to 3rd. But the new hire didn’t have gifted-and-talented certification.

In observations, she’d sit in the back of the classroom with an absolutely unreadable face, and I’d spend the whole lesson spiraling. But that was the thing: she actually watched, and she actually paid attention.

I avoid it like the plague, and if I’m honest, that single trait alone probably cancels out any other quality I have that might make me good in the role. But in her ever-reassuring way, she insisted I had the right skill set and spent the following two years encouraging me to move beyond the classroom.

Declining enrollment hit this school hard, and once again I had to leave a school and community I loved, despite my principal’s best attempts to advocate to keep me. Year 20: All of the Above Before landing here, I feared education had turned into something that wasn’t sustainable, and that the leaders of the past were just that.

They made sure every child could say out loud, “I feel safe and seen here,” and mean it, not just say it because it was expected. And these women, who I am so lucky to have had in my life, were the great ones.

t: AI: Helping Students Join the Conversation
q: At the recent Oracy Conference here in my college at Cambridge, Hughes Hall, I found myself talking with Kate Paradine, CEO of Voice 21, about the new report, chaired by Estelle Morris, on why white working-class children are being left behind in education. Mothers in Grimsby interviewed by the BBC were saying that what mattered to them was not “education”, but work.

In my college I meet people working in medicine, law, architecture, engineering, business and public policy, most of them deeply engaged with hospitals, industry, government and communities. If even Cambridge, supposedly the peak of academia, is full of people connecting knowledge with practice, why does school still feel to so many families as if it is a detour from reality?

Why should this be reserved for adults already inside elite professional worlds? Imagine a mathematics lesson in which students run a market stall — pricing stock, working out wastage, and deciding whether to extend credit to a regular customer, while a rival stallholder undercuts them and the council warden threatens a fine.

The idea is to augment the existing knowledge-focused curriculum — perhaps accelerated with AI but with teachers guiding and framing throughout — and to show how that knowledge can be applied to understand real world situations and solve real world problems. Most of what human beings learn, we do not learn from books or formal lessons.

My own work on dialogic education has been inspired partly by Michael Oakeshott, who taught history for many years at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and described education as joining “the conversation of mankind”. But we need to widen Oakeshott’s image beyond history, philosophy and classics.
We inherit long conversations: mathematics, science, history, literature, technology, craft, politics, religion and work. They are living traditions of argument, evidence, judgement and practice.
The third loop is deferred indefinitely: learn this now, you may need it later. AI-supported, multi-voiced cases could bring all three loops together.
